review_method: Assistant-authored editorial synthesis of official abstracts and explicitly cited full-text passages; no independent replication. Selected, non-exhaustive reading guide; tags are not population labels.

papers.title: The Effect of Intrinsic Dataset Properties on Generalization: Unraveling Learning Differences Between Natural and Medical Images
papers.question: Why can natural-image and medical-image generalization behave differently?
papers.finding: Intrinsic dimension and label sharpness help explain the different learning behavior of the tested natural and medical image datasets.
papers.evidence: Theory and comparisons across six models and eleven datasets examine dataset properties rather than introducing an architecture alone.
papers.scope: A partial explanation for these datasets, not a theorem covering all medical modalities or all transfer failures.

papers.title: Robustness of Deep Learning for Accelerated MRI: Benefits of Diverse Training Data
papers.question: Does specializing MRI reconstruction training to one acquisition distribution improve robustness?
papers.finding: Diverse training distributions improve effective robustness to tested shifts; joint training can match specialized models on their own distributions.
papers.evidence: Comparisons include U-net, ViT, and VarNet; joint-data experiments include a smaller joint-set control, and OOD comparisons condition on in-distribution performance.
papers.scope: Accelerated MRI reconstruction, measured mainly by reconstruction quality. This does not establish diagnostic safety or that every data mixture helps.
papers.evidence_location: Sections 3–4, PDF pp. 5–7 (joint-set control and effective-robustness analysis)

papers.title: Do We Really Need Message Passing in Brain Network Modeling?
papers.question: Is standard message passing well matched to correlation-based brain graphs?
papers.finding: When topology and node features reuse the constructed connectivity information, the tested GNN and Transformer operators may add little; a simple classifier is a strong diagnostic baseline.
papers.evidence: Graph-construction analysis and ABIDE/ADNI comparisons motivate a quadratic alternative, BQN; the paper also analyzes its community-detection behavior.
papers.scope: The finding depends on the Pearson-correlation construction and chosen node features. It does not show all message passing is unnecessary for brain data.

papers.title: From Pretraining to Pathology: How Noise Leads to Catastrophic Inheritance in Medical Models
papers.question: Can pretraining noise leave harmful effects after medical fine-tuning?
papers.finding: Controlled pretraining corruption produces downstream medical OOD degradation; higher-order feature statistics provide an empirical account of the inherited effect.
papers.evidence: Varying label corruption during pretraining, downstream medical comparisons, and regularization interventions test the proposed explanation.
papers.scope: The tested corruption regimes and datasets bound the claim. The feature-statistic account is not a universal causal proof about all noisy pretraining.
papers.evidence_location: Introduction and Sections 2.1–2.3, including the controlled corruption setup

papers.title: Is Limited Participant Diversity Impeding EEG-based Machine Learning?
papers.question: Can more EEG segments from the same people substitute for more participants?
papers.finding: Participant diversity limits scaling on some tasks, but the trade-off differs across datasets: additional segments can compensate substantially in the tested sleep-staging setting.
papers.evidence: Participant/segment budget comparisons across tasks and models, followed by augmentation and self-supervised-learning investigations.
papers.scope: Results differ between TUAB/CAUEEG and PhysioNet. Do not simplify this to “more segments never help” or a universal EEG scaling law.
papers.evidence_location: Sections 3.4–3.5 and 4.1–4.3 (especially the task-dependent segment trade-off)

papers.title: Accounting For Informative Sampling When Learning to Forecast Treatment Outcomes Over Time
papers.question: What changes when patient observation frequency depends on clinical history?
papers.finding: Informative observation timing induces a mismatch between the observed training objective and the desired outcome-forecasting objective.
papers.evidence: A formal sampling model yields inverse-intensity weighting; a continuous-time forecasting method illustrates the correction.
papers.scope: Identification relies on sampling-at-random and causal assumptions, including treatment unconfoundedness. This is not clinical validation of counterfactual treatment effects.

papers.title: Context Clues: Evaluating Long Context Models for Clinical Prediction Tasks on EHR Data
papers.question: Which properties of clinical event sequences challenge long-context models?
papers.finding: Repetition, irregular event timing, and later timeline complexity expose differences from natural-language sequence modeling; tested longer-context models are more resilient on downstream tasks.
papers.evidence: EHR-OMOP sequence analysis and EHRSHOT performance stratification examine these factors alongside context-length comparisons.
papers.scope: Stratified associations do not by themselves prove causation. Findings concern the tested event-based EHR models and tasks, not every clinical text model.
papers.evidence_location: Sections 4.2–4.4 (repetition, irregular timing, and timeline position)

papers.title: BrainBits: How Much of the Brain are Generative Reconstruction Methods Using?
papers.question: Does realistic brain-to-image reconstruction mean the model recovered more neural information?
papers.finding: Visual quality can reflect generative priors rather than information supplied by the brain measurements.
papers.evidence: Information bottlenecks probe how much neural input reconstruction systems actually use.
papers.scope: This diagnoses the tested generative reconstruction systems; it does not show neural input is irrelevant to every brain-decoding approach.

papers.title: Rethinking Cross-Subject Data Splitting for Brain-to-Text Decoding
papers.question: Can a cross-subject split still leak information in brain-to-text evaluation?
papers.finding: Subject separation alone need not prevent leakage through other shared structure in the evaluated datasets.
papers.evidence: The paper analyzes splitting practices and re-evaluates decoding under revised criteria.
papers.scope: The scope is the analyzed datasets and split designs; do not infer every brain-to-text result leaks.

papers.title: Every Component Counts: Rethinking the Measure of Success for Medical Semantic Segmentation in Multi-Instance Segmentation Tasks
papers.track: AAAI Technical Track on Computer Vision III
papers.question: Do aggregate segmentation metrics reflect success on every lesion instance?
papers.finding: Large components can dominate aggregate scores and obscure failures on smaller components in multi-instance medical segmentation.
papers.evidence: Component-level analysis motivates an evaluation protocol that gives individual instances explicit attention.
papers.scope: The concern is multi-instance objectives and component weighting, not evidence that overlap metrics are useless for every segmentation task.

papers.title: Pattern Recognition or Medical Knowledge? The Problem with Multiple-Choice Questions in Medicine
papers.question: How much medical MCQ performance can come from answer-format patterns?
papers.finding: Models can answer questions about fictional medical content surprisingly well; choice and answer-length cues can support performance without the presumed medical knowledge.
papers.evidence: Synthetic-organ textbooks and bilingual MCQs, plus answer-only, reasoning, and length ablations, probe alternative explanations.
papers.scope: This is a controlled synthetic-MCQ stress test. It does not establish that models lack medical knowledge; some ablations use a narrower set of models.

papers.title: MediConfusion: Can you trust your AI radiologist? Probing the reliability of multimodal medical foundation models
papers.question: Can medical multimodal models distinguish images requiring opposite answers to the same question?
papers.finding: Deliberately selected confusing image pairs expose failures hidden by easier conventional medical VQA evaluations.
papers.evidence: ROCO pairs are selected using high BiomedCLIP similarity and lower DINOv2 similarity; 352 questions are evaluated with individual and paired-set accuracy.
papers.scope: This is adversarially curated, not a prevalence estimate for routine clinical images. Paired-set accuracy and individual accuracy have different random baselines.
papers.evidence_location: Sections 2.1–2.3 (pair selection and individual versus set metrics)

papers.title: ReEvalMed: Rethinking Medical Report Evaluation by Aligning Metrics with Real-World Clinical Judgment
papers.question: Do report metrics distinguish clinically meaningful changes from harmless rewrites?
papers.finding: Controlled rewrites expose mismatches between clinical significance and the behavior of established report-evaluation metrics.
papers.evidence: Expert-validated report pairs test discrimination and robustness to clinically significant versus insignificant changes.
papers.scope: Constructed report perturbations and the evaluated clinical-report setting limit generalization; no metric is established as valid for all clinical language.

papers.title: Automated Metrics for Medical Multi-Document Summarization Disagree with Human Evaluations
papers.question: Do automatic medical summarization metrics rank systems as humans do?
papers.finding: The evaluated automatic metrics can disagree with human judgments; some system rankings are negatively correlated.
papers.evidence: Comparing automatic scores against human evaluation tests whether common optimization targets measure the intended summarization quality.
papers.scope: Medical multi-document summarization and the assessed metrics/systems bound the result. Do not claim every automatic metric is universally anticorrelated with humans.

papers.title: Not What the Doctor Ordered: Surveying LLM-based De-identification and Quantifying Clinical Information Loss
papers.question: Do strong de-identification scores guarantee preservation of clinical information?
papers.finding: High token-level scores can coexist with over-redaction and clinically relevant changes; standard scores and simple retention proxies miss important errors.
papers.evidence: Survey, multiple de-identification pipelines, manual clinical-change annotations, and a clinical-information-retention evaluation method.
papers.scope: Manual change rates use selected false-positive cases, not all notes. Results depend on AHS/MIMIC-III, annotation schemas, and the evaluated pipelines.

papers.title: Spurious Correlations and Beyond: Understanding and Mitigating Shortcut Learning in SDOH Extraction with Large Language Models
papers.question: Can unrelated substance mentions trigger unsupported drug-use extraction?
papers.finding: Alcohol and smoking mentions are associated with false drug-status predictions; trigger-removal experiments support a shortcut explanation in this setting.
papers.evidence: Drug-status extraction tests vary triggers, prompting, fine-tuning, and demographic strata; evidence-focused prompts are explored as mitigation.
papers.scope: ACL short paper; a focused MIMIC-SHAC case study. The suggested origin in pretraining is a hypothesis, not an established mechanism.
papers.evidence_location: Evaluation framework and Sections 4–6, including trigger removal and gender-stratified results

papers.title: The Boundaries of Fair AI in Medical Image Prognosis: A Causal Perspective
papers.question: Do existing fairness methods transfer reliably to image-based prognosis?
papers.finding: Time-to-event models exhibit group performance gaps; the benchmark finds limits to existing mitigation strategies and examines their sensitivity to distribution shift.
papers.evidence: FairTTE covers multiple imaging modalities, prognosis outcomes, sensitive attributes, and fairness measures; model-selection and group-gap analyses make the audit explicit.
papers.scope: Fairness depends on the metric, dataset, and outcome. This is not a universal impossibility theorem for fair prognosis; shift mechanisms need separate scrutiny.
papers.evidence_location: Abstract and experimental setup/results in PDF p. 7; detailed shift claims remain abstract-level

papers.title: Revisiting MAE Pre-training for 3D Medical Image Segmentation
papers.question: Why have MAE pretraining results been inconsistent for 3D medical segmentation?
papers.finding: Data, architecture, and evaluation choices matter; a carefully configured pipeline changes conclusions about the value of MAE pretraining.
papers.evidence: The study combines systematic evaluation with an optimized pretraining and segmentation recipe.
papers.scope: Substantial method contribution, with a brain-MRI focus. Treat as a hybrid, not pure evidence that MAE universally fails or succeeds in medical imaging.

papers.title: Revisiting End-to-End Learning with Slide-level Supervision in Computational Pathology
papers.question: Why can sparse-attention MIL impair end-to-end pathology encoder adaptation?
papers.finding: Sparse attention can over-focus on redundant patches or miss discriminative instances during joint optimization, despite working well with strong frozen features.
papers.evidence: The paper analyzes this training risk and introduces ABMILX with local/global attention and an end-to-end sampling pipeline.
papers.scope: Problem analysis is intertwined with a substantial architecture/training proposal; the finding is not a rejection of all MIL or sparse attention.
papers.evidence_location: Introduction, Section 3.1 and Section 3.2 (optimization risks and ABMILX)

papers.title: Position: Reinforcement Learning in Dynamic Treatment Regimes Needs Critical Reexamination
papers.question: How stable are offline RL conclusions for dynamic treatment regimes?
papers.finding: Algorithm rankings change with reward, MDP, and off-policy evaluation choices; naive policies can score well under some estimators.
papers.evidence: The authors report over 17,000 evaluations on a sepsis dataset and argue for more reliable evaluation practice.
papers.scope: This is a position paper with empirical support. Favorable estimated returns do not show random treatment is clinically better.
papers.evidence_location: Abstract and main-results discussion of naive baselines and evaluation sensitivity

papers.title: Position: Medical Large Language Model Benchmarks Should Prioritize Construct Validity
papers.question: Does a medical benchmark score measure the clinical capability it claims to measure?
papers.finding: Proof-of-concept studies find gaps between common medical benchmark performance and the intended clinical constructs.
papers.evidence: Construct-validity analysis includes matching MedQA items to clinical encounters and testing criterion validity.
papers.scope: A position paper with selected empirical demonstrations, not comprehensive validation of every medical benchmark. Clinical proxy tasks and scoring choices matter.
papers.evidence_location: Introduction and Section 4.1 (criterion validity of MedQA)
